# R & the Shell {#sec-r-command-line}

In this chapter, we will learn to 

- execute shell commands from R
- execute shell script in RStudio
- execute shell commands in RMarkdown
- execute R commands & script in the shell

## R 

Now, let us turn our attention to executing commands from R using `system2()`. 
Here we will focus on the following

- execute a command without arguments
- execute commands with arguments
- redirect output

Let us try to execute a command without any additional arguments. We will execute the `ls` command to list all files and directories. Use `system2()` and specify the command using the `command` argument. Whenever you execute a command from R, the first argument is the command, and it must be enclosed in quotes.

```{r eval=FALSE}
system2(command = "ls")
```

Great! Now, how do we specify the options? The additional options of a 
command must be stored as a character vector and specified using the `args`
argument. In the example below, we delete the `myexamples` folder we created earlier while decompressing the `zip_example.zip` file.

```{r eval=FALSE}
system2(command = "rm",
        args    = c("-r", "myexamples"))
```

In some cases, we might want to redirect the output. Let us say we are writing a 
message to a file using the `echo` command; we want the output redirected to the 
`release.txt` file. The `stdout` argument can be used to redirect output to a file or the R console. In the below example, we redirect the output to a file.

```{r system2_3a, eval=FALSE}
system2(command = "echo", 
        args    = c("Great Truth"), 
        stdout  = "release.txt")
```

In the next example, we redirect the output to the R console by setting the value of the `stdout` argument to `TRUE`. If you are curious, set the value to `FALSE` and see what happens.

```{r system2_4a, eval=FALSE}
system2(command = "diff", 
        args    = c("imports_olsrr.txt", "imports_blorr.txt"),  
        stdout  = TRUE)
```

The `run()` command from the [processx](https://processx.r-lib.org/) package can be used to execute shell commands as well.

## RStudio 

In RStudio, commands can be executed from shell scripts by pressing `Ctrl + Enter`. Instead of sending the command to the R console, it is redirected to 
the terminal where it is executed as shown below.

![Running shell commands from an RStudio shell script with Ctrl+Enter](img/cline_rstudio_shell.gif){#fig-rstudio-shell fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## RMarkdown 

RMarkdown supports `bash`, `sh` and `awk`. This book was initially created using `sh`, as the underlying operating system is Windows. Later, we used `bash` after installing the Windows subsystem for Linux. Click [here](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/language-engines.html#shell-scripts) to learn more.

![Using the bash language engine in RMarkdown](img/cline_shell_markdown.png){#fig-shell-markdown fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Rscript

In this section, we will learn to execute R commands and scripts in the command line using:

- `R -e`
- `Rscript -e`
- `R CMD BATCH`

The `-e` option allows us to specify R expression(s). `R -e` will launch R and then execute the code specified within quotes. Use semi-colon to execute multiple expressions as shown below. You will be able to run the below commands only if you are able to launch R from the command line. Windows users need to ensure that R is added to the path environment.

```{sh c118a, eval=FALSE}
R -e "head(mtcars); tail(mtcars)"
```

`Rscript -e` will run code without launching R.

```{sh c119a, eval=FALSE}
Rscript -e "head(mtcars)"
```

We can use `Rscript` to execute a R script as well. In the example below, we execute the code in the `analysis.R` file. 

```{sh c120a, eval=FALSE}
Rscript analysis.R
```

If you are more interested, try the [littler](https://cran.r-project.org/package=littler) package as well.

## Exercises

1. From R, run `system2(command = "ls")` to list files, then `system2(command = "rm", args = c("-r", "myexamples"))` as shown in the chapter. State what you expect in the R console and in the working directory in each case.
2. From R, run `system2(command = "echo", args = c("Great Truth"), stdout = "release.txt")`, then check `release.txt` contains the text. Then run `system2(command = "diff", args = c("imports_olsrr.txt", "imports_blorr.txt"), stdout = TRUE)` and note the differences print to the R console instead of a file. Clean up `release.txt` afterwards if it is not part of the fixtures.
3. From the shell, run `Rscript -e "head(mtcars)"` and `Rscript analysis.R`, and compare with `R -e "head(mtcars); tail(mtcars)"`. State the expected difference: running code without launching the full R console versus executing a script file.

Worked solutions in `solutions/r-shell.md` (attempt first).
